edited_rows.rationale: The row opens on the hallel’s imperative summons, הַ֥לְלוּ יָ֨הּ הַ֭לְלוּ עַבְדֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה הַֽ֝לְלוּ אֶת שֵׁ֥ם יְהוָֽה (web:Ps.113.1 = oshb:Ps.113.1, “Praise Yah! Praise, you servants of Yahweh, praise Yahweh’s name”), the psalm’s verse-initial hallelu-Yah opener, and continues through declarative praise—יְהִ֤י שֵׁ֣ם יְהוָ֣ה מְבֹרָ֑ךְ (web:Ps.113.2 = oshb:Ps.113.2, “Blessed be Yahweh’s name”) to רָ֖ם עַל כָּל גּוֹיִ֥ם יְהוָ֑ה (web:Ps.113.4 = oshb:Ps.113.4, “Yahweh is high above all nations”). The unit closes where the register shifts from imperative summons and declarative praise to a rhetorical question at web:Ps.113.5.

observed_substrate_signals: triple imperative opens הַ֥לְלוּ יָ֨הּ הַ֭לְלוּ עַבְדֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה הַֽ֝לְלוּ (oshb:Ps.113.1), the verse-initial hallelu-Yah frame member (inventory: 11 verse-initial occurrences book-wide)

edited_rows.rationale: The row opens on the turn to direct address, מַה לְּךָ֣ הַ֭יָּם כִּ֣י תָנ֑וּס (web:Ps.114.5 = oshb:Ps.114.5, “What was it, you sea, that you fled?”), a second-person apostrophe repeating web:Ps.114.3’s third-person report (הַיָּ֣ם רָ֭אָה וַיָּנֹ֑ס, oshb:Ps.114.3, “The sea saw it, and fled”) as a direct question. The address extends to the mountains (הֶֽ֭הָרִים תִּרְקְד֣וּ כְאֵילִ֑ים, oshb:Ps.114.6) and to the earth itself, מִלִּפְנֵ֣י אָ֭דוֹן ח֣וּלִי אָ֑רֶץ (web:Ps.114.7 = oshb:Ps.114.7, “Tremble, you earth, at the presence of the Lord”), before the closing relative-clause description of the rock-to-pool wonder (web:Ps.114.8) reverts to third person.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting the address-to-the-waters (web:Ps.114.5-Ps.114.6) from the address-to-the-earth-and-closing-wonder (web:Ps.114.7-Ps.114.8) was considered but rejected because both remain within one continuous second-person apostrophe opened at web:Ps.114.5, with no addressee or mood break between them.
observed_substrate_signals: second-person apostrophe מַה לְּךָ֣ הַ֭יָּם כִּ֣י תָנ֑וּס opens oshb:Ps.114.5, directly repeating oshb:Ps.114.3's third-person report (הַיָּ֣ם רָ֭אָה וַיָּנֹ֑ס) as a question
the 2fs imperative ח֣וּלִי (word index 2, addressing "earth" which follows at word index 3) addresses the earth directly within oshb:Ps.114.7's quoted span מִלִּפְנֵ֣י אָ֭דוֹן ח֣וּלִי אָ֑רֶץ
closing relative-clause description at oshb:Ps.114.8 reverts to third-person, closing the psalm
edited_rows.device_notes: The address-to-the-sea turn at 114:5 is this psalm's structural hinge, repeating 114:3's third-person report as direct second-person apostrophe.

edited_rows.rationale: The psalm opens with a doubled self-effacing petition, “Not to us, Yahweh, not to us, but to your name give glory” (web:Ps.115.1), pivots to the nations' taunting question, “Where is their God, now?” (web:Ps.115.2), and answers it with a counter-affirmation of divine freedom, “But our God is in the heavens. He does whatever he pleases” (web:Ps.115.3). The three verses form one rhetorical unit -- petition, taunt, retort -- before the idol catalogue opens at web:Ps.115.4 with עֲֽ֭צַבֵּיהֶם (oshb:Ps.115.4) ('their idols'), a third-person description with no addressee, unlike v1's second-person address to Yahweh (2ms suffixes throughout); v3's own "our God is in the heavens, he does whatever he pleases" is itself first-person-plural-plus-third-person narration, not address, but still distinct in register from the idols' bare third-person description.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: A row spanning web:Ps.115.1-Ps.115.8 could fold the retort into the idol polemic it provokes, but the address shifts from second person to Yahweh (vv1,3) to third-person idol description (v4ff), marking a seam at 3|4.
observed_substrate_signals: web:Ps.115.1's doubled negation has no title pseudo-verse preceding it -- Ps 115 is untitled, and no WEB title pseudo-verse exists for it in the verse map
web:Ps.115.2's question אַיֵּה נָ֝֗א אֱלֹהֵיהֶֽם (oshb:Ps.115.2) is answered directly by web:Ps.115.3's assertion וֵֽאלֹהֵ֥ינוּ בַשָּׁמָ֑יִם (oshb:Ps.115.3) that God is in the heavens
edited_rows.device_notes: All of Psalm 115's rows meet in one parent. The psalm opens without a superscription, so this opening row is also the psalm's opening Hebrew content.

edited_rows.rationale: The idol polemic runs as one catalogue: idols are מַ֝עֲשֵׂ֗ה יְדֵ֣י אָדָֽם (oshb:Ps.115.4) ('the work of men's hands') with mouths that don't speak, eyes that don't see, ears that don't hear, noses that don't smell, hands that don't feel, and feet that don't walk (web:Ps.115.5-7), before the maker/trust indictment closes it, “Those who make them will be like them; yes, everyone who trusts in them” (web:Ps.115.8). The catalogue's cola (e.g. פֶּֽה לָ֭הֶם וְלֹ֣א יְדַבֵּ֑רוּ עֵינַ֥יִם לָ֝הֶ֗ם וְלֹ֣א יִרְאֽוּ (oshb:Ps.115.5)) share one noun-then-negated-verb syntax across web:Ps.115.5-7 through 115:7's first two cola ("their hands, they don't feel" / "their feet, they don't walk"); the pattern breaks at 115:7's own third colon ("nor do they speak through their throat," negative-verb-first with no leading body-part noun) -- the catalogue still runs as one unbroken unit through the seam at 8|9, just not on a fully uniform syntax; the closing verb כֹּ֭ל אֲשֶׁר בֹּטֵ֣חַ בָּהֶֽם (oshb:Ps.115.8) ('everyone who trusts in them') catches on the imperative יִ֭שְׂרָאֵל בְּטַ֣ח (oshb:Ps.115.9) ('Israel, trust!') that opens the next strophe, marking the seam at 8|9.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting the sense-organ catalogue (vv5-7) from its opening (v4) and closing indictment (v8) would fragment one anaphoric list across three rows with no independent tier-1 seam between them.
observed_substrate_signals: the 3 sense-organ cola of web:Ps.115.5-7 pair a body-part noun with a negated verb apiece, e.g. אָזְנַ֣יִם לָ֭הֶם וְלֹ֣א יִשְׁמָ֑עוּ אַ֥ף לָ֝הֶ֗ם וְלֹ֣א יְרִיחֽוּן (oshb:Ps.115.6), in the same pattern (sweep: 3 verses)

web:Ps.115.8's closing root (כֹּ֭ל אֲשֶׁר בֹּטֵ֣חַ בָּהֶֽם (oshb:Ps.115.8), 'everyone who trusts in them') recurs as the imperative opening web:Ps.115.9 (יִ֭שְׂרָאֵל בְּטַ֣ח (oshb:Ps.115.9), 'Israel, trust!')
edited_rows.device_notes: The maker/trust catchword bridges idols and Yahweh across the row seam at 8|9: the psalm's argument turns on the same root used initially for misplaced trust, then for rightly placed trust.

edited_rows.rationale: Three vocatives receive a shared two-part formula (3 times) in turn -- an imperative to trust in Yahweh (singular at 115:9, plural at 115:10-11) followed by the closing clause “He is their help and their shield” -- which alone is byte-identical across all 3 verses -- addressed to Israel (יִ֭שְׂרָאֵל (oshb:Ps.115.9), web:Ps.115.9), the house of Aaron (בֵּ֣ית אַ֭הֲרֹן (oshb:Ps.115.10), web:Ps.115.10), and those who fear Yahweh (יִרְאֵ֣י יְ֭הוָה (oshb:Ps.115.11), web:Ps.115.11); the closing refrain (עֶזְרָ֖ם וּמָגִנָּ֣ם הֽוּא (oshb:Ps.115.9)) is byte-identical (collate.py, byte tier) across all 3 verses. The same three-member roster recurs at web:Ps.118.2-Ps.118.4 with a jussive 'let…say' verb replacing the imperative; the fixed collocation בֵּ֣ית אַ֭הֲרֹן (oshb:Ps.115.10) sweeps to 4 verses book-wide and יִרְאֵ֣י יְ֭הוָה (oshb:Ps.115.11) to 6 verses book-wide, both concentrated in this recurring triad (Ps 135:19-Ps 135:20, outside this span, inserts a fourth member, house of Levi, before repeating the fearers clause).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Treating vv9-11 as three separate one-verse rows would split one triadic (3-member) refrain unit whose members share one closing clause verbatim (byte tier, 3 verses).
observed_substrate_signals: the refrain עֶזְרָ֖ם וּמָגִנָּ֣ם הֽוּא (oshb:Ps.115.10) (sweep: 3 verses, web:Ps.115.9-11) closes each of the three vocatives identically at byte tier

בֵּ֣ית אַ֭הֲרֹן (oshb:Ps.115.10) sweeps to 4 verses book-wide (skeleton, sweep.py) and יִרְאֵ֣י יְ֭הוָה (oshb:Ps.115.11) to 6 verses book-wide, both fixed collocations concentrated in this triad and its recurrences
edited_rows.device_notes: The Israel / house of Aaron / fearers-of-Yahweh triad is the psalm's central structuring device, returning as a bless-declaration triad at web:Ps.115.12-13 and, differently worded, at web:Ps.118.2-4.

edited_rows.rationale: The verb יְבָ֫רֵ֥ךְ (oshb:Ps.115.12) ('he will bless') repeats across a second, narrated triad -- “He will bless the house of Israel. He will bless the house of Aaron” (web:Ps.115.12), “He will bless those who fear Yahweh, both small and great” (web:Ps.115.13) -- before the strophe widens into a direct blessing on the congregation, “May Yahweh increase you more and more” (web:Ps.115.14) and “Blessed are you by Yahweh, who made heaven and earth” (web:Ps.115.15). The root behind יְ֭בָרֵךְ (oshb:Ps.115.13) occurs 4 finite times across web:Ps.115.12-13 alone, mirroring the trust-triad's three-member roster in narrated rather than imperative form before the address widens at v14.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Breaking the narrated bless-triad (vv12-13) from the widened blessing that follows (vv14-15) is a genuine rival: 115:14 shifts to 2mp address ('increase you', x2) and 115:15 opens with the 2mp independent pronoun 'you' -- a real addressee-register change at 13|14, not the absence an earlier reading of this seam claimed. The row nonetheless keeps 12-15 together because the 'bless' root (oshb:Ps.115.12 x3, oshb:Ps.115.13 x1) that opens the narrated triad reappears at oshb:Ps.115.15's 'blessed are you,' framing the whole span as one blessing-movement from narration to direct declaration; the seam is live, and this reading is held at medium confidence.
observed_substrate_signals: יְהוָה֮ זְכָרָ֪נוּ יְבָ֫רֵ֥ךְ יְ֭בָרֵךְ אֶת בֵּ֣ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל יְ֝בָרֵ֗ךְ אֶת בֵּ֥ית אַהֲרֹֽן (oshb:Ps.115.12) carries the root ברך three times in one verse, and יְ֭בָרֵךְ (oshb:Ps.115.13) once more opening v13 -- 4 finite occurrences across the two verses

web:Ps.115.15's participle עֹ֝שֵׂ֗ה שָׁמַ֥יִם וָאָֽרֶץ (oshb:Ps.115.15) ('who made heaven and earth') supplies the heaven/earth vocabulary that web:Ps.115.16 picks up immediately after this row's close
edited_rows.device_notes: The bless-triad (vv12-13) answers the trust-triad (vv9-11) member for member, narrating what the imperative called for.

edited_rows.rationale: The heaven/earth antithesis (“The heavens are Yahweh's heavens, but he has given the earth to the children of men” web:Ps.115.16) sets up a second antithesis between the silent dead and the blessing living: לֹ֣א הַ֭מֵּתִים יְהַֽלְלוּ יָ֑הּ וְ֝לֹ֗א כָּל יֹרְדֵ֥י דוּמָֽה (oshb:Ps.115.17) (“The dead don't praise Yah,” web:Ps.115.17) against “but we will bless Yah, from this time forward and forever more. Praise Yah!” (web:Ps.115.18). The closing הַֽלְלוּ יָֽהּ (oshb:Ps.115.18) is verse-final -- the psalm's sole hallelu-Yah occurrence among its 18 verses; it is byte-distinct from v17's יְהַֽלְלוּ יָ֑הּ (oshb:Ps.115.17) -- a different, imperfect verb form ('they will praise') rather than the imperative liturgical formula.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Grouping v16 with the preceding blessing strophe (ending v15) is possible since both touch heaven/earth language, but v16 restates the theme as an independent cosmological claim rather than a continuation of the second-person blessing of v14-15.
observed_substrate_signals: a skeleton sweep of the hallelu-Yah collocation returns 26 verses book-wide (sweep.py --skel); two of those are not the imperative liturgical formula -- web:Ps.115.17 is the imperfect verb יְהַֽלְלוּ (oshb:Ps.115.17) ('they will praise'), and oshb:Ps.22.27 is a skeleton-only collision (a 3mp-imperfect plus the full divine name, not the imperative-plus-Yah idiom) -- leaving 24 imperative-frame instances (11 verse-initial + 13 verse-final), the disclosure inventory's ratified count

web:Ps.115.18 carries 1 paseq per the marks inventory (single-witness; a bare count disclosure, not a positional claim -- the inventory records no offset/word-index for paseq occurrences); corroborating texture, not a boundary driver
edited_rows.device_notes: The living/dead antithesis of vv17-18 closes the psalm's argument begun at v1: those who bless Yah's name (not the silent dead) are the psalm's speaking community.

edited_rows.rationale: The thanksgiving opens with a love-declaration and its ground, “I love Yahweh, because he listens to my voice” (web:Ps.116.1) and “I will call on him as long as I live” (web:Ps.116.2), then narrates the crisis that provoked the calling -- “The cords of death surrounded me… I found trouble and sorrow” (web:Ps.116.3) -- closing on the quoted cry itself, אָנָּ֥ה יְ֝הוָ֗ה מַלְּטָ֥ה נַפְשִֽׁי (oshb:Ps.116.4) ('Yahweh, I beg you, deliver my soul,' web:Ps.116.4).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: A shorter row ending at v2 (declaration alone) would separate the reason for loving Yahweh from the crisis-and-cry narrative that the declaration's 'therefore' (v2) sets up.
observed_substrate_signals: web:Ps.116.1-2 gives the ground clause (כִּֽי יִשְׁמַ֥ע יְהוָ֑ה, oshb:Ps.116.1, 'because he listens') and the resulting resolve (therefore I will call) before the crisis is narrated at v3
web:Ps.116.4's cry, אָנָּ֥ה יְ֝הוָ֗ה מַלְּטָ֥ה נַפְשִֽׁי (oshb:Ps.116.4), is the psalm's opening quoted direct speech, closing the opening movement
edited_rows.device_notes: Psalm 116, taken whole, is this row set's parent. Psalm 116 moves from a love-declaration through a crisis-and-deliverance report into a doubled vow movement (vv13-14 mirrored at vv17-18).

edited_rows.rationale: Yahweh's character is stated generally -- “Yahweh is gracious and righteous… Yahweh preserves the simple” (web:Ps.116.5-6) -- before the speaker addresses their own soul, שׁוּבִ֣י נַ֭פְשִׁי (oshb:Ps.116.7) (“Return to your rest, my soul,” web:Ps.116.7), reports the deliverance in three parts, “my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from falling” (web:Ps.116.8), and resolves to “walk before Yahweh in the land of the living” (web:Ps.116.9).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Ending the row at v7 (self-address alone) would separate the resolve 'return to your rest' from the report of deliverance it anticipates in v8.
observed_substrate_signals: נַפְשִֽׁי (oshb:Ps.116.4, 'my soul') occurs at 116:4 (word index 6), again in the self-address שׁוּבִ֣י נַ֭פְשִׁי (oshb:Ps.116.7) of v7, and again at oshb:Ps.116.8 (word index 2, נַפְשִׁ֗י) in the deliverance report -- 3 verse occurrences of the soul-noun (oshb:Ps.116.4, oshb:Ps.116.7, oshb:Ps.116.8) threading the crisis-to-report movement, the earliest at 116:4 (disclosed as cross-seam texture, not a driver here)

web:Ps.116.7's imperative self-address שׁוּבִ֣י (oshb:Ps.116.7) ('return') addresses the speaker's own soul, a distinct addressee from Yahweh; the psalm's next self-address is the servant self-naming at 116:16
edited_rows.device_notes: The soul-address device (v7) frames this row's report of deliverance, resolving into the resolve-to-walk clause of v9.

edited_rows.rationale: A reflective aside on the affliction just survived -- “I believed, therefore I said, "I was greatly afflicted."” (web:Ps.116.10) and “I said in my haste, "All people are liars."” (web:Ps.116.11) -- leads into the pivotal question that launches the vow movement, “What will I give to Yahweh for all his benefits toward me?” (web:Ps.116.12).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Attaching v12's question to the following cup-of-salvation verse (v13) as its answer is defensible, but the question itself closes the reflective aside begun at v10 and is the strophe's rhetorical hinge rather than the start of the vow's content.
observed_substrate_signals: web:Ps.116.10-11 (הֶ֭אֱמַנְתִּי כִּ֣י אֲדַבֵּ֑ר אֲ֝נִ֗י עָנִ֥יתִי מְאֹֽד (oshb:Ps.116.10) … אֲ֭נִי אָמַ֣רְתִּי בְחָפְזִ֑י כָּֽל הָאָדָ֥ם כֹּזֵֽב (oshb:Ps.116.11)) is a well-known crux in Hebrew syntax -- the exact logical relation between 'I believed' and the quoted self-report is debated among translations -- a content difficulty distinct from the row's boundary, which rests on the aside's self-contained question-and-answer shape

web:Ps.116.12's question מָֽה אָשִׁ֥יב (oshb:Ps.116.12) ('what will I give') has no grammatical antecedent in vv10-11, which themselves carry no divine-name token at all -- the same feature that makes v13's answer ('I will take the cup...') a live continuation; the row keeps v12 with the aside because its interrogative form, not its content, closes the self-contained question-and-answer shape of vv10-12 rather than opening the vow's declarative content
edited_rows.device_notes: The reflective aside (vv10-11) is the psalm's hinge between the deliverance report and the vow movement that the question of v12 opens.

edited_rows.rationale: The opening vow half-strophe begins, כּוֹס יְשׁוּע֥וֹת (oshb:Ps.116.13) (“I will take the cup of salvation,” web:Ps.116.13), closing on וּבְשֵׁ֖ם יְהוָ֣ה אֶקְרָֽא (oshb:Ps.116.13) ('and call on Yahweh's name') then the vow-payment formula (web:Ps.116.14); an interlude on death's value follows, “Precious in Yahweh's sight is the death of his saints” (web:Ps.116.15), and the speaker names themself “your servant, the son of your servant girl” (עַ֭בְדְּךָ בֶּן אֲמָתֶ֑ךָ, oshb:Ps.116.16, web:Ps.116.16), immediately followed by “You have freed me from my chains” (פִּ֝תַּ֗חְתָּ לְמוֹסֵרָֽי, oshb:Ps.116.16, web:Ps.116.16). The vow-payment clause closing v14 (נְ֭דָרַי לַיהוָ֣ה אֲשַׁלֵּ֑ם נֶגְדָה נָּ֝֗א לְכָל עַמּֽוֹ (oshb:Ps.116.14)) matches the one closing v18 at byte tier (collate.py; 2 verses), marking vv13-14 as one half of a matched pair whose other half opens the next row.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Ending the row at v14 (cup and opening vow alone) would isolate the servant self-naming of v16, which the row keeps attached despite v15's intervening third-person nominal clause ("Precious in Yahweh's sight is the death of his saints") breaking any direct grammatical continuity; v13 itself names Yahweh in the third person rather than addressing him, so the connective thread through 13-16 is thematic (vow-and-service) rather than a single uninterrupted address.
observed_substrate_signals: web:Ps.116.14's vow clause (נְ֭דָרַי לַיהוָ֣ה אֲשַׁלֵּ֑ם נֶגְדָה נָּ֝֗א לְכָל עַמּֽוֹ (oshb:Ps.116.14)) is byte-identical (2 verses) to web:Ps.116.18's (נְ֭דָרַי לַיהוָ֣ה אֲשַׁלֵּ֑ם נֶגְדָה נָּ֝֗א לְכָל עַמּֽוֹ (oshb:Ps.116.18))

edited_rows.rationale: An antiphonal gate scene: פִּתְחוּ לִ֥י שַׁעֲרֵי צֶ֑דֶק אָֽבֹא בָ֝ם אוֹדֶ֥ה יָֽהּ (oshb:Ps.118.19) (“Open to me the gates of righteousness. I will enter into them. I will give thanks to Yah.” web:Ps.118.19) is a plea addressed to unnamed gatekeepers, answered by זֶֽה הַשַּׁ֥עַר לַיהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.118.20) (“This is the gate of Yahweh; the righteous will enter into it.” web:Ps.118.20) -- a declarative reply in a different grammatical voice, third person rather than imperative-to-second-person -- before the speaker's own thanksgiving resumes at web:Ps.118.21.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Reading v19 alone as the close of the preceding testimony strophe is possible, but its imperative plea 'open to me' has no addressee across the preceding 5 verses (118:14-18) and instead opens a new liturgical scene answered by v20.
observed_substrate_signals: the gate scene shifts grammatical voice twice within 2 verses: second-person imperative plea (v19) to third-person declarative reply (v20) to first-person resumed testimony (v21); a comparable plea/reply/testimony movement recurs later in the psalm at 118:25-26/27/28, sharing the same 2ms thanksgiving-verb tie (a skeleton sweep of the form used at 118:21 and 118:28 returns exactly 2 verses book-wide), so this pattern is the psalm's clearest instance rather than its only one
שַׁעֲרֵי צֶ֑דֶק (oshb:Ps.118.19) ('gates of righteousness,' v19) and הַשַּׁ֥עַר לַיהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.118.20) ('the gate of Yahweh,' v20) are the psalm's 2 gate references, both inside this row
edited_rows.device_notes: This row is Psalm 118's sharpest antiphonal seam (2 verses), argued from the voice return: plea, then reply in a distinct grammatical voice.

edited_rows.rationale: Three interpretive declarations follow the preceding scene: אֶ֭בֶן מָאֲס֣וּ הַבּוֹנִ֑ים הָ֝יְתָ֗ה לְרֹ֣אשׁ פִּנָּֽה (oshb:Ps.118.22) (“The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.” web:Ps.118.22), “This is Yahweh's doing. It is marvelous in our eyes” (web:Ps.118.23 = oshb:Ps.118.23, whose Hebrew demonstrative זֹּ֑את sits at word index 3, not the verse-initial position its English rendering suggests), together with “This is the day that Yahweh has made. We will rejoice and be glad in it!” (web:Ps.118.24 = oshb:Ps.118.24, the row's only genuinely verse-initial demonstrative, זֶה) -- a triad of interpretive sayings rather than the antiphonal request-and-reply shape of the gate scene at 118:19-21. The verse-initial demonstrative device itself is not what unites the triad -- a book-wide sweep finds it only at 118:20 and 118:24, so it actually straddles this row's own opening seam at 118:21|118:22 (118:20 sits in the preceding row) rather than running through all three of this row's verses. The triad's own unity rests on its shared interpretive-declaration shape and its position after the gate liturgy, not on a verse-initial demonstrative.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Attaching the rejected-stone saying (v22) to the gate scene that precedes it is possible on liturgical-procession grounds, but v22 introduces a fresh image (building, not gate) interpreted by the This-is sayings of vv23-24 rather than continuing the gate dialogue.
observed_substrate_signals: of web:Ps.118.22-24, only v24 opens with a genuine demonstrative (זֶה הַ֭יּוֹם, oshb:Ps.118.24, naming the festal day); v23's demonstrative זֹּ֑את (oshb:Ps.118.23) names the stone's reversal but sits at word index 3, after the opening prepositional phrase מֵאֵ֣ת יְ֭הוָה ('from Yahweh'); v22 has no demonstrative at all

the rejected-stone saying's original setting (building metaphor, royal or communal) is not settled by the row's own bytes; the referent of 'the stone' is an open interpretive question this candidate holds rather than resolves
edited_rows.device_notes: The This-is triad (vv22-24) interprets the reversal just enacted, sitting between the gate liturgy (vv19-21) and the festal procession (vv25-27).

edited_rows.rationale: A hosanna plea, אָנָּ֣א יְ֭הוָה הוֹשִׁ֘יעָ֥ה נָּ֑א (oshb:Ps.118.25) (“Save us now, we beg you, Yahweh!” web:Ps.118.25), is met by a blessing acclamation, בָּר֣וּךְ הַ֭בָּא בְּשֵׁ֣ם יְהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.118.26) (“Blessed is he who comes in Yahweh's name!” web:Ps.118.26) spoken in a different grammatical voice than the plea it answers, before the procession moves to the altar, “Bind the sacrifice with cords, even to the horns of the altar” (web:Ps.118.27).

edited_rows.device_notes: The festal-procession scene (vv25-27) is the psalm's second antiphonal moment, moving from plea to acclamation to altar instruction.

You are my God, I will exalt you.”) -- names God with two distinct Hebrew words (אֵלִ֣י, אֱ֝לֹהַ֗י) that WEB renders identically as "You are my God," the doubling a rendering effect rather than a repeated Hebrew lexeme -- closes the psalm with its opening line repeated verbatim: הוֹד֣וּ לַיהוָ֣ה כִּי ט֑וֹב כִּ֖י לְעוֹלָ֣ם חַסְדּֽוֹ (oshb:Ps.118.29) is byte-identical (collate.py, byte tier) to הוֹד֣וּ לַיהוָ֣ה כִּי ט֑וֹב כִּ֖י לְעוֹלָ֣ם חַסְדּֽוֹ (oshb:Ps.118.1), a true hodu inclusio framing all 29 verses of the psalm.
